name: Israeli Sign Language
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Israeli Sign Language (isra1236) is not in the catalog. The three Glottolog items are really two works, both by Sandler (with Nespor): 'Prosody in Israeli Sign Language' (Language and Speech 42, 1999; Glottolog lists it twice, once under the preprint title 'Prosodic phonology in ISL' 1998) and 'The medium and the message' (Sign Language & Linguistics 2, 1999). Both were obtained openly from the University of Haifa Sign Language Research Lab media library (signlab.haifa.ac.il; the older sandlersignlab host refuses connections), saved with text extractions under and logged in there; two further Sandler papers from the same site (1999b on cliticization/prosodic words; 2010 TPS overview) were read for completeness. All are about phrasal prosody, not word stress: ISL signs are mostly monosyllabic prosodic words, so no word-internal stress placement is stated anywhere; the papers establish phrase-final prominence (rightmost sign of the phonological phrase, marked by hold/reduplication/pause; intonational-phrase-final by size and slowness) and facial 'intonation'. Nothing remains to acquire (priority none); the DOI landing pages (SAGE, Benjamins) are paywalled but unnecessary.

new_statements.quote: If the establishment of the prominence relations among the sister constituents of the phonological phrase is governed by (5) in sign languages, as in spoken languages, and if the basic order of ISL is head-complement, as shown in (22), then the rightmost sign of P should be strong and its sister signs weak. This appears to be the case. We are considering the physical correlates of phonological phrase prominence, all realized with the hands, to be the following: hold, reduplication, and pause. [...] All but 30 of the 247 potential phonological phrases had one of these markers on the last word. If these are indeed prominence markers, then the vast majority of phonological phrases in our corpus had prominence at the end.
new_statements.citation: Nespor, Marina & Wendy Sandler (1999). Prosody in Israeli Sign Language. Language and Speech 42(2-3): 143-176 (author preprint, University of Haifa Sign Language Research Lab; same work as Glottolog 637032 'Prosodic phonology in Israeli Sign Language')
new_statements.locator: §3.2.1 'Grouping and prominence', preprint pp. 17-18 (published pagination 143-176, exact page not verified); abstract p. 1
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (36-page author preprint, header 'published in Language & Speech 42: 2&3. 1999. 143-176') and its. The quoted passage is present verbatim in section 3.2.1 'Grouping and prominence': the first sentence ('If the establishment of the prominence relations among the sister constituents') sits at the foot of preprint p. 17 (PDF page 17) and the rest ('of the phonological phrase is governed by (5).. hold, reduplication, and pause' and 'All but 30 of the 247 potential phonological phrases had one of these markers on the last word. If these are indeed prominence markers, then the vast majority of phonological phrases in our corpus had prominence at the end.') on preprint p. 18 (PDF page 18);…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No word-level stress rule is described for ISL in any opened source. Signs are canonically monosyllabic (one movement), so the only prominence described is phrasal: the last sign of each phonological phrase is strong (ISL is head-complement, so prominence is right-edge), marked by hold, reduplication of the sign, or a following pause; the intonational phrase likewise has final prominence, and narrow focus is moved to I-final position rather than stressed in situ.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not applicable / not discussed; the three phrase-final prominence markers (hold, reduplication, pause) almost never co-occur.
new_statements.exceptions: 30 of 247 phonological phrases in the corpus lacked a prominence marker on the last sign; pronoun clitics cannot bear phrase-level prominence by themselves and coalesce with the preceding host (Sandler 1999b p. 250); lexically reduplicated signs drop their reduplication when not phrase-final. Contrastive focus may keep in-situ prosodic marking.
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological phrase and intonational phrase in elicited sentences; the authors say the prominence claim 'needs to be confirmed experimentally'. Sign language: spoken-word stress is inapplicable; the word (single sign) is not a stress domain in these descriptions.
new_statements.identity_note: Israeli Sign Language (isra1236), the sign language of the Israeli Deaf community; the sources describe ISL as a whole (Haifa-area native consultants), no dialect specified. Sandler, Belsitzman & Meir 2020 compares ISL with Al-Sayyid Bedouin Sign Language (alsa1242), a different language. Note for the catalog: this is a signed language; the quoted statement concerns phrase-level prominence, not word stress.

We are considering the physical correlates of phonological phrase prominence, all realized with the hands, to be the following: hold, reduplication, and pause. [...] All but 30 of the 247 potential phonological phrases had one of these markers on the last word. If these are indeed prominence markers, then the vast majority of phonological phrases in our corpus had prominence at the end.
new_statements.citation: Nespor, Marina & Wendy Sandler (1999). Prosody in Israeli Sign Language. Language and Speech 42(2-3): 143-176 (author preprint from signlab.haifa.ac.il; Glottolog 637032/637033)
new_statements.locator: section 3.2.1 'Grouping and prominence', preprint p. 18 (journal pp. c. 157-158); monosyllabicity of signs at section 2.1, preprint p. 12
new_statements.reading: ISL has no word-stress rule in the spoken-language sense: signs are (mostly) monosyllabic prosodic words (preprint p. 12), so there is no word-internal stress locus, and the authors' own results concern phrase-level prominence only. Prominence falls on the rightmost sign of the phonological phrase (head-complement language), realized manually by hold, reduplication or pause on that sign (216 of 247 phrases), and on the final sign of the intonational phrase by larger, slower signing; focus is marked by moving the focused constituent to I-final position, not by in-situ stress shift (preprint p. 25). If the catalog ever takes sign languages, ISL should be coded 'word stress not applicable (monosyllabic signs); phrasal prominence phrase-final' with this source, not as a fixed or weight-based stress system.

sources.note: Phrase-level only: prominence falls on the rightmost (last) sign of the phonological phrase (ISL is head-complement), cued by hold, reduplication or pause (217 of 247 phrases); intonational-phrase prominence is final, focus moved to I-final position rather than stressed in situ. sources.citation: Nespor, Marina and Sandler, Wendy (1998). Prosodic phonology in Israeli Sign Language. Language and Speech, 143-176. [Glottolog 637032, listed by Glottolog as a phonology]
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request); access check: online with a university library login
sources.quote: It is generally agreed that the phonology of sign language includes a syllable-like unit and that the movement corresponds to the syllable peak (Coulter 1982; Wilbur 1982; this volume; Brentari 1990, 1999; Perlmutter, 1992; Sandler 1993a). Taken together with constraints on the structure of signs, these observations mean that most signs are monosyllabic. It is argued, in Sandler (1999) that this monosyllabic unit is the optimal form of the prosodic word in sign languages.
sources.locator: author preprint, header 'published in Language & Speech 42: 2&3. 1999. 143-176'; section 2.1 (MS p. 12) and section 3.2.1 'Grouping and prominence' (MS pp. 16-19), 3.2.3 Summary (MS p. 21)
sources.note: Same work as Glottolog 637033 (the lab site files it under the 1998 title; the PDF header gives the published title 'Prosody in Israeli Sign Language', Language and Speech 42(2-3), 1999, 143-176). The paper contains no statement of word-level stress placement: ISL signs are described as (mostly) monosyllabic prosodic words (MS p. 12), so there is no word-internal stress locus to state. What it does establish is PHRASAL prominence: ISL is head-complement, and 'the rightmost sign of P should be strong and its sister signs weak. sources.citation: Sandler, Wendy (2010). Prosody and syntax in sign languages. Transactions of the Philological Society 108(3), 298-328. [not in search list; read for stress remarks]
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: Little is said here about stress / prominence. The reader is referred to Wilbur (1999), Nespor & Sandler (1999), van der Kooij, Crasborn, & Emmerik (2006), and Sandler (to appear a) for investigations and discussions of this issue in different sign languages.
sources.locator: PDF p. 10 (journal p. c. 307), footnote 9; PDF p. 5 footnote 4
sources.note: p. 307 n. 9: 'Little is said here about stress/prominence', refers to Wilbur (1999, ASL), Nespor & Sandler (1999), van der Kooij et al. (2006, NGT) and Sandler (to appear, 'The visual prosody of sign language'); n. 4 notes Klima & Bellugi's ASL compound stress on the second member. Phrase-final prominence in ISL restated.

sources.citation: Sandler, Wendy (2008). The syllable in sign language: Considering the other natural language modality. In B. L. Davis & K. Zajdo (eds.), The Syllable in Speech Production, 379-407. New York: Taylor & Francis.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: pp. 391-393: stress facts given are for ASL (second syllable of compounds stressed, Klima & Bellugi 1979; first syllable of reduplicated nominals, Supalla & Newport 1978); sign syllables show no onset-rhyme weight asymmetry; intonational tunes align with whole phrases, 'not a single syllable within it, stressed or otherwise' (citing Nespor & Sandler 1999). No ISL word-stress statement.

sources.citation: Sandler, Wendy (1999a). The medium and the message: Prosodic interpretation of linguistic content in Israeli Sign Language. Sign Language & Linguistics 2(2), 187-215. [Glottolog 643349]
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: In this preliminary study, it was found that phonological phrases conform to the algorithm in (9), and prominence is at the end, as predicted, since ISL appears to be basically a head-complement language. The correlates of prominence are argued to be reduplication, hold at the end of the prominent sign, or pause after the last word in the phonological phrase.
sources.locator: section 2.1 'The prosodic word' pp. 192-193; section 2.2 'The phonological phrase' pp. 199-200
sources.note: General discussion of rhythm, prominence and intonation; 'the word is also the domain of lexical stress assignment' stated for spoken language only; ISL prominence treated at phrase level (footnote 5 cites Wilbur: ASL pronouns not stressed phrase-finally). No ISL word-stress rule.

sources.citation: Sandler, Wendy (1999b). Cliticization and prosodic words in a sign language. In T. A. Hall & U. Kleinhenz (eds.), Studies on the Phonological Word, 223-254. Amsterdam: Benjamins. [not in search list; found on the Haifa sign-lab site during this search of works with stress in the title]
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: We discovered the following correlates of rhythmic prominence in ISL, which appears to be a right-branching language: (1) Prominence is marked on the rightmost word of a phonological phrase, mainly by holding the hand still at the end of a sign and/or reduplicating the sign. (2) Prominence is marked on the rightmost word of an intonational phrase with size and rate of signing (large and slow is more prominent).
sources.locator: p. 239 (section on prosodic structure), p. 242, p. 250
sources.note: Optimal prosodic word = one monosyllabic sign; pronoun clitics coalesce with a host at the right edge of the phonological phrase 'because they are in a prosodically prominent position but cannot get phrase level stress by themselves' (p. 250); 'stress assignment can only see lexical categories' (p. 242, citing Wilbur for ASL). Phrase-level prominence only.
